text: An event subscription was created in the system's object management infrastructure so that a shell launches whenever a file appears in a watched folder
The attacker registered a recurring job with the operating system's built-in job facility that downloads a file every night at 3 AM
A line was added to the user's periodic job table so the collector runs every five minutes
A hidden console window executed a decoded command string without any script file on disk
A shell process was spawned with arguments that run a one-line pipeline of commands passed directly on the command line
A process opened a handle to the service that stores authentication secrets and read its memory to recover account hashes
The same user's password was guessed dozens of times in quick succession from a single workstation
The malicious payload was hidden inside an otherwise harmless image file that looked legitimate on disk
Employees received emails containing a document attachment that installed the first stage when opened
The controller channel was hidden inside normal web requests sent to a domain that looks like a legitimate content provider
Outbound callbacks were relayed through a publicly available tunneling service to hide the real destination
The dropper fetched the next stage of the implant over the network into a temporary folder
A kernel hook was installed so that the implant's files do not appear when other processes list the directory
The most recent restore points were deleted to make it impossible to roll the system back to a clean state
Right after the privilege change, the traces of the activity were scrubbed from the event logs and leftover files
A dormant local account that had not been used for a year was re-enabled and given local administrator rights
A new entry in the system's service database was installed so the backdoor launches automatically at every boot
A legitimate process was started in a frozen state, its memory was swapped out for the malicious image, and it was then released
A trusted system binary was observed loading a dynamically linked library from the user's profile directory
The host protection tool was stopped and its reporting disabled before the group moved to the next server
The file was named with a leading dot so that standard directory listings do not show it
A built-in utility of the operating system was repurposed to fetch and run a script from an internal web address
From the compromised box the attacker logged into a second host using the desktop sharing protocol on port 3389
The collected files were sent back to the operator through the same connection that receives the commands
Chunks of the database dump were smuggled out of the network hidden inside domain name lookups
Instructions for the implant were encoded into the names of domain lookups sent to an attacker-controlled name server
The code ran entirely in the process memory without ever writing an executable to the disk
The implant ran a series of system queries to learn the operating system, the machine name, and the domain it belongs to
The compromised host scanned the local address range to find other machines it could reach
The payload listed all running programs to identify which one belongs to the database service
The malware walked through the directory tree looking for office documents to mark for upload
A trojanized shared library was placed in a directory that the system searches before the real one, so the wrong module loads
The intrusion started with the password of a legitimate service account that the attacker had found in a config file
An RSA private key file found on a laptop was used to log in to a production host without a password
Saved website logins were extracted from the web application where the user keeps their credentials
Target files were copied into a temporary folder to be packed and uploaded in one go
Backup files were shredded so the organization cannot restore the data after the incident
The upload of the stolen data was deliberately paced in small bursts to stay under the bandwidth alert threshold
File modification times were altered so the dropped artifact looks like it belongs with files from last year
The service process took on the identity of the highest-privilege local account to open protected resources
wmic.exe process creation and WMI event subscriptions
schtasks.exe creating scheduled tasks
rundll32.exe loading unsigned DLLs from profile
execution of whoami and w to identify the logged in user
Mimikatz reading lsass.exe memory
Base64 and Hex encoded C2 traffic
SetWindowLong calls modifying Extra Window Memory
low-level hooks on keyboard APIs GetAsyncKeyState SetWindowsHookEx
